idiom_name: sealed interface (unexported marker method) + type switch
implementation_notes: Go has no sum types and no exhaustiveness checking, so the closure is expressed structurally: an interface whose method set includes an unexported marker (`type Payment interface{ isPayment() }`) can only be satisfied by types declared in the same package, which closes the variant set; each variant is an ordinary struct with unexported fields plus a constructor function, which is how Go approximates immutability (no exported setters, cheap copying). Elimination is a type switch, and completeness is not compiler-verified - the guarantee must be added by tooling such as `//sumtype:decl` with go-check-sumtype, sumlint, or an exhaustive switch whose `default` panics or returns an error, checked in CI. A typed enum (const block plus a `String` method) is the simpler answer when variants carry no data, and generics do not close the gap because a type parameter over the sealed interface still cannot be matched exhaustively.
pitfalls: A `nil` interface is a state no variant covers: type switches need an explicit `nil`/default arm (the linters demand one) or a nil payment panics far from its construction site.

Mixing receivers for the marker (`func (Card) isPayment()` vs `func (*Transfer) isPayment()`) changes which types satisfy the interface, so a `*Transfer` value falls into the default arm while tests using `Transfer{}` pass.
Exported fields are writable by every holder: immutability is a package convention (unexported fields, constructors, copy-on-write), not a language guarantee.
